documents.abstract: With the creation of China’s National Integrated Pipeline Network and the transition to natural gas energy measurement, quality fluctuations caused by multisource gas mixing pose severe challenges to trade fairness and pipeline network safety. As a key technology for achieving accurate energy measurement, natural gas quality tracking has undergone a paradigm shift: from steady-state hydraulic calculations to transient composition tracking, and then to intelligent modeling paradigms that feature mechanism-data-driven collaboration. Through a systematic review of technological developments and an analysis of core algorithms, this paper highlights the core value of this technology, namely, its ability to significantly reduce reliance on online gas chromatographs, thereby providing a technical solution to promote energy measurement at Class B and C station yards. It further explores the new challenges presented by hydrogen-blended natural gas and other novel gas sources, including property calculations, numerical dissipation, and safety assessments. Ultimately, future research on this technology should focus on the deep integration of mechanistic models and artificial intelligence, propelling quality-tracking technology toward high precision, strong real-time capabilities, and wide adaptability. This review aims to provide a theoretical reference and technical support for the development of China’s self-sufficient, controllable natural gas energy measurement system.

Modern society is undergoing rapid educational changes driven by technological evolution and rising academic demands, establishing Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) as key tools for teaching English as a Foreign Language (EFL). This study evaluates the use of AI tools to enhance oral production (speaking skills) among 107 eighth-grade students (sections A, B, and C) at the *Unidad Educativa Fiscal Bicentenario D7 Vespertino* in Quito, Ecuador. The methodology employed a quantitative, descriptive field study design. Key diagnostic findings reveal that 73% of students struggle with initial oral fluency, and 75% report frequent pronunciation errors. However, 68% state that practicing with AI tools boosts their confidence and significantly reduces communication anxiety when speaking in public. Furthermore, 70% demonstrate high motivation for learning through technological resources. Critical limitations identified include limited instructional time (three hours per week), a lack of independent practice outside the classroom (75%), and recurring connectivity and infrastructure issues (56%). The study concludes that overcoming these barriers and the digital divide requires the design and implementation of low-data adaptive micro-learning modules, independent practice guides, and continuous teacher training workshops.

Abstract The rapid evolution of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) has transformed the landscape of intelligent web application development. Despite their remarkable fluency, standalone LLMs frequently suffer from hallucination, outdated knowledge, and an inability to reference verifiable, domain-specific information, which limits their reliability in enterprise contexts. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these limitations by coupling a parametric language model with a non-parametric retrieval mechanism that fetches relevant information from an external knowledge base at inference time. This paper presents the design, methodology, and prototype architecture of a RAG-based generative AI web application intended to demonstrate how retrieval, semantic search, and prompt engineering can be combined with modern web development practices to build context-aware, factually grounded AI systems. The proposed system integrates a document ingestion and chunking pipeline, sentence-level embedding generation, a vector database for high-dimensional semantic search, and a large language model layer responsible for grounded response generation. The web application is designed using a React.js/Next.js frontend, a FastAPI/Node.js backend, JWT-based authentication, and a cloud-native deployment strategy using Docker, Kubernetes, and CI/CD pipelines on platforms such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud Platform. The paper reviews recent literature on RAG architectures, compares leading vector databases (Pinecone, FAISS, ChromaDB, Milvus) and embedding models, and surveys contributions from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta AI, Microsoft Research, Hugging Face, LangChain, and LlamaIndex. Rather than reporting fabricated experimental numbers, this work proposes a rigorous evaluation methodology — covering retrieval accuracy, groundedness, latency, and user satisfaction — that can be applied once the prototype is fully deployed. The study concludes that RAG-based architectures offer a practical, scalable, and enterprise-ready pathway toward building trustworthy generative AI web applications, while identifying open challenges such as embedding quality, context-window constraints, and operational cost that motivate future work in agentic and multimodal RAG systems. Keywords: Generative AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Large Language Models (LLMs), Prompt Engineering, Vector Database, Semantic Search, AI Chatbot, Web Development, Cloud Deployment, Enterprise Applications.

LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have demonstrated strong capabilities in solving complex problems across diverse domains. Recently, the dynamic orchestration of agent systems has become an important research direction. However, existing methods suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, restricting their ability to adapt to reasoning requirements during execution. To address these limitations, we reframe MAS design as a partially observable Markov decision process, in which both the composition and scale of the MAS are dynamically determined. We propose DHCG, a novel framework that coordinates three modules (Planner, Worker, and Generator) to progressively construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch based on the query and evolving execution feedback. At each step, guided by feedback, the Planner generates a set of distinct and complementary roles tailored to the current reasoning needs and selectively routes relevant information to each role. It can also finalize the hierarchical collaboration graph early or progressively expand it when additional reasoning is required. We further introduce action-aware preference optimization to train the Planner to make more effective decisions when constructing hierarchical collaboration graphs. We systematically evaluate DHCG across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks. DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance among the compared methods, improving over the single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and outperforming both static and dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77-8.02 points. Additional experiments further demonstrate its generalization across different Planner backbones and unseen Worker models.

Real-world settings involve multiple interacting cognitive states such as mental workload, drowsiness, fatigue, and mind wandering, yet these are typically studied in isolation. A critical question is whether these states can be empirically differentiated given that they share overlapping behavioral and physiological signatures. We investigated whether task difficulty and sleep restriction produce dissociable effects across these states, and whether their response patterns reflect distinct underlying mechanisms or a common cognitive resource using a unified framework. Participants from operational populations (Study 1: n = 40; Study 2: n = 27) performed three complementary tasks (MATB-II, N-Back, and SART) under two manipulations: task difficulty and partial sleep restriction, targeting cognitive load and alertness. Increasing task difficulty degraded performance and increased perceived workload and fatigue across tasks. In contrast, sleep restriction primarily elevated subjective drowsiness and mind wandering, with smaller, task-dependent effects on performance. These findings provide evidence that cognitive and physiological states influencing situational awareness can be differentiated using complementary manipulations and characterized through distinct behavioral and subjective measures. This distinction provides a foundation for future predictive and monitoring approaches in applied settings.

Abstract This paper examines the association between digital communication at work and employee well-being, moderated by occupational status and the fulfillment of basic psychological needs. Two studies were conducted to investigate these relationships. Study 1 utilized data from the European Social Survey, encompassing 25 countries ( N = 24,331). Study 2 involved a longitudinal survey of Finnish workers ( N = 1817) collected at nine time points over 6-month intervals from 2019 to 2023. Multilevel regression models were employed to analyze the data. Study 1 found that digital communication positively correlates with job satisfaction in Europe, with a stronger effect observed among lower-position workers. Study 2 revealed that the use of digital platforms was associated with higher work engagement and women reported significantly higher work engagement than men. However, for higher-position office workers, particularly those in supervisory roles, increased use of organizational social media platforms and excessive social media use were linked to decreased work engagement. Several interaction effects indicated that the association between digital communication as well as digital tool use and work engagement and job satisfaction is contingent on basic psychological need satisfaction and occupational status. Organizations should tailor their digital communication strategies to account for employees’ occupational status and work autonomy. This paper addresses a gap in cross-national and longitudinal research on the impact of digital communication on workplace well-being. It provides insights into how digital communication tools differentially affect employees based on their occupational status and psychological needs.

This chapter examines digital communication, marketing, and institutional identity in higher education as interconnected organisational domains. It treats digitalisation as the foundation of institutional practice and digital communication as a managerial rather than purely promotional function. Institutional communication is analysed as an integrated process encompassing both external stakeholder engagement and internal communication. The chapter reviews the core platforms that underpin institutional communication, including websites, social media, email, and internal collaboration systems. It argues that strategic effectiveness depends less on the number of channels used than on their governance as a coherent, audience-centred portfolio. It also explores the role of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs), podcasts, and EdTech tools, which increasingly combine communication, service delivery, and data generation. The chapter further considers how artificial intelligence is reshaping higher education marketing through personalisation, predictive analytics, and customer relationship management (CRM-)based engagement, while highlighting the importance of trust, transparency, and regulatory compliance. Finally, it argues that successful implementation depends on digital leadership, effective governance, capability development, and staff well-being, all of which shape whether digital transformation strengthens or weakens institutional coherence.

Digital research ecosystems (DREs) constitute the infrastructure core of contemporary academic scholarship, significantly altering how scientific knowledge is generated, organised, validated, and preserved. This comprehensive academic work provides an exhaustive, multi-layered analysis of DREs as integrated sociotechnical systems operating at the intersection of computational advancement and institutional evolution. It examines the historical shift towards data-intensive science, maps the emergence of the fourth paradigm of discovery, and investigates how these ecosystems support the lifecycle of research data through the operationalisation of open science principles. The structural components of DREs are dissected across multiple layers, emphasising the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and automated knowledge systems in semantic discovery and automated curation. Furthermore, the analysis addresses critical systemic challenges, including technological fragmentation, academic capitalism, data silos, geopolitical digital inequalities, and the delicate ethical-legal tensions surrounding data privacy, surveillance, and security. Finally, it outlines emerging revolutionary paradigms such as Decentralised Science (DeSci) and autonomous, closed-loop research infrastructure, providing a robust theoretical framework for understanding the long-term trajectory of global scientific collaboration.

In the modern era, the survival of traditional sports disciplines is directly linked to their ability to adapt to a dynamic media environment. The International Shooting Sport Federation (ISSF) has entered a period of fundamental transformation, shifting from a closed technical discipline toward a high-demand global media product. The central challenge lies in changing the "cognitive perception" of shooting – transforming a process that appears static to an outside observer into an emotionally resonant and technologically accessible spectacle. This article analyzes the key directions of this process. First, it examines the diversification of content delivery through the aggressive scaling of digital presence and the exploration of new platforms. A vital aspect is the technological verification and increased transparency of officiating, achieved through the implementation of VAR objective control systems and "live aiming" shot visualization technologies. The study also investigates the integration of virtual reality and esports as a means of creating alternative "entry points" into the sport via digital simulators. Alongside these developments, the work analyses the associated risks and institutional consequences of this transformation. The implementation of innovations such as AI-driven hit analysis and VR tools fosters the necessary "immersive connection" between the athlete and the fan. This is critical for attracting sponsorship capital, as it allows dry technical data to be converted into engaging content. The findings are based on a comparative analysis of Redtorch reports (SportOnSocial 2025), official ISSF press releases, and current industry publications. Keywords: ISSF; VAR; live aiming; User Generated Content (UGC); TikTok; Douyin; virtual reality; e-sport; OBS, artificial Intelligence (AI), digital transformation

This study explored artificial intelligence (AI) research assistants through the lens of scholars from different disciplines as they interacted with the tools. The goal was to determine whether AI tools provide relevant scholarly literature or prioritize surface-level relevance at the expense of disciplinary depth, and to examine how scholars perceive the usefulness of the tools in teaching and learning. The study used a multiple-phase, qualitative design in which ten scholars from several disciplines completed structured search tasks in each AI research assistant (Consensus, Elicit, SciSpace), followed by semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed using qualitative coding techniques, with themes developed through thematic analysis approach. Analysis involved data familiarization, memoing, iterative first and second cycle coding, and the generation and refinement of themes. The findings revealed six themes from the search task diaries and interviews with participants: article coverage varied across disciplines; discipline specific information needs and resource mismatch; a complementary resource for scholarly article discovery; AI summaries technically correct but generic; faculty perceptions on AI tools in student learning; usability and cognitive load considerations. The findings indicate that while most tools surfaced additional research from scholarly journals, they often did not consistently identify seminal literature across the sampled disciplines. AI summaries on the literature were perceived as factually correct but generic. Lastly, participants expressed varied perceptions about the ways in which the tools could be used in teaching and learning contexts.

Abstract This study investigates the discourse characteristics of AI-generated argumentative essays designed to simulate student writing, comparing them with human-authored texts to explore linguistic variation and its implications for academic discourse. While large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT demonstrate impressive fluency and coherence, questions remain about their capacity to engage in nuanced argumentation and the critical reasoning expected in academic contexts. Employing Biber’s (1988) multidimensional (MD) analysis, this study examines systematic differences between LLM-generated and human-written essays across dimensions of register variation, informational density, syntactic complexity, and persuasion. The results reveal that ChatGPT essays are markedly more informationally dense, context-independent, and abstract, yet exhibit reduced interpersonal engagement and overt persuasion compared with student essays. The paper concludes by reflecting on broader pedagogical and ethical implications for the integration of AI tools into academic writing and corpus-based research.

On-policy distillation (OPD) has attracted growing attention as an effective way to transfer capabilities from teacher models to student models. Recent studies further explore OPD as a tool for improving large language model safety with promising results. However, these approaches typically assume that the teacher and training data are trustworthy. In this paper, we uncover an overlooked threat to OPD for safety: a safety-aligned but backdoored teacher can propagate its hidden malicious behavior to an initially clean student. Under our threat model, a poisoning rate as low as 3% results in an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 70% on the distilled student. We further identify two training choices that can amplify this risk. First, increasing the number of training epochs can lead to high ASR even at low poisoning rates. With only 10 poisoned samples, ASR reaches 67% after 16 epochs. Second, the commonly used top-k KL can accelerate backdoor transfer, causing trigger-conditioned harmful behavior to emerge earlier than sampled-token KL in most settings. Alongside these findings, we explore a simple mitigation, Lazy Defense, which clips KL rewards to make student updates less aggressive, limiting aggressive updates and slowing backdoor learning. Experiments show that Lazy Defense delays backdoor transfer in low poisoning rate settings. Together, our findings reveal that OPD can propagate backdoors, highlighting the need to address the safety risks of OPD.

Activation steering provides a lightweight and flexible way to control large language model (LLM) behavior. However, effective steering requires more than inducing the intended behavior: it should also limit unintended changes and remain robust across inputs and training data. Existing evaluations cover these dimensions only in fragments. As a result, the trade-offs between efficacy and side effects have not been systematically characterized. We introduce SteerScope, a two-axis, multi-dimensional evaluation suite that jointly characterizes steering outcomes and method properties through 15 metrics. We score target efficacy and side effects on language quality, task capabilities, and safety and reliability, and further assess generalization and data dependence through steering-specific metrics for sample efficiency and sample sensitivity. Rather than comparing methods at a single operating point, we characterize the trade-offs between efficacy and side effects. Under matched models, tasks, and evaluation protocols, we benchmark 23 methods spanning 4 families, including prompting, LoRA, and SFT as baseline methods, and release the suite as an extensible codebase. We find that current activation steering methods do not yet surpass the Prompt Steering baseline in their overall balance between steering efficacy and side effects: across both model scales, no evaluated activation steering method achieves higher efficacy without incurring greater composite side effects. We further uncover a consistent coupling between steering efficacy and side effects. Under OOD prompts, target efficacy is often preserved, whereas side effects tend to become more pronounced, particularly through declines in instruction relevance and fluency. Methods also exhibit sharply different sample-efficiency profiles.

This treatise is composed of the author's previously unpublished position papers and material on the vibrational physics:This work formulates a fundamental alternative to classical evolutionary biology and astrophysics by consistently subordinating biological, geological, and cosmological phenomena to the laws of vibrational physics, electrodynamics, and quantum optics. Instead of attributing evolutionary developments to random mutations and cosmic states to infinite singularities, the model describes the universe as a thermodynamic steady state within global electromagnetic dipole fields. The organic body—conceived as an electronic "state cloud"—interacts as a living dipole via the skin, a programmable vibrational membrane, with terrestrial field voltages and cosmic photon streams. Along this gradient, a global three-sphere model is derived, possessing universal validity for human pigmentation, the vertical evolution of bipedalism and dipole balancing (dinosaurs, primates), and the geometry of flora. While the high-energy southern sphere (positive pole exit) functions as a creative generator for the emergence and stabilization of complex archetypal patterns, the photon-poor northern sphere (negative pole entry) is defined as a defensive protective and reflective zone that maintains existing energetic blueprints through maximum photon scattering ("white" skin). Similarly, solid celestial bodies behave like planetary batteries, whose poles, acting as thermodynamic cooling circuits, enforce a state of vibrational deprivation (crystallization/ice). Movement on Earth is defined as a unified field theory of the locomotion of living beings on Earth. To avoid deterministic fallacies, the theory strictly separates physical-biological evolution from cognitive-cultural information evolution. Civilizational progress is explained by the concentration of external data storage ("archive.txt") and the establishment of heritable file paths, culminating in a global technological homeostasis within the triangle of humans, AI, and robotics. Finally, the model scales these principles to interstellar cosmology: Stars in their plasma state possess incompletely differentiated, fluctuating poles due to convective currents. Only during the transition to a highly compressed stage is an irreversible polar alignment forced. At the extreme point of a black hole, this abrupt differentiation leads to an extreme field stress that tears the system apart in the mode of a cosmic dipole discharge. The system mutates from a state of maximum absorption (black hole) to a state of maximum emission (white hole) – the physical explanation for the phenomenon of the supernova as well as the Big Bang.

While generative AI models can produce visually faithful artwork, they often fall short in conveying emotional authenticity--a key driver of human expression. In visual storytelling, particularly comic storyboarding, this gap becomes pronounced: effective storyboards require both technical knowledge (e.g., anatomical accuracy or scenic composition) and emotional insight (from lived experience). We explore how human-AI collaboration can support emotion-driven creativity, where the user's feelings guide generation and emotional resonance is the goal. We present EmoToon, a technology probe that helps non-professional artists generate sketch-like storyboards and iterate on visual ideas. In a controlled study with N=25 participants, we find that AI assistance significantly improves emotional expression, aesthetic quality, and exploration, but reduces users' creative ownership. Our findings offer broader insights for human-AI co-creation in the domain of comic storytelling, emphasizing balance between output quality and user freedom, and raising new challenges for image generation models in this domain.

Automated vehicles (AV) can exhibit diverse driving behaviors that deviate from driver expectations. More research is needed to understand drivers’ preferred driving styles when navigating safety-critical situations as well as their responses to unexpected AV driving behaviors. Forty-eight participants experienced simulated automated driving scenarios where an AV navigated a construction zone while exhibiting four different predefined driving styles that varied in terms of cautiousness and efficiency. After each trial, participants provided feedback to adjust the AV’s driving style toward their preferences, which was successfully implemented in 80% cases. Drivers’ trust, workload, voluntary takeover decisions, eye movements, and skin conductance were measured. Overall, participants preferred driving styles balancing cautiousness and efficiency. When AV behavior matched driver preferences, they reported higher trust and more stable visual scanning patterns, while unexpected behaviors were associated with broader ocular scanning. Findings can inform the development of adaptive systems that intelligently modify AV behaviors.

A stroke results in a serious disability due to sudden disruption in blood flow to the brain, which may cause fatal outcomes and is considered as the topmost cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide. The reduction of brain damage along with the recovery of patients has shown potential increase due to accurate and time based diagnosis. The competence of artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning and for stroke detection using data from different sources such as EHRs, EEG, and MRI have been explored in this chapter. Different types of CNN and deep learning models are analyzed to classify various data types along with the identification of stroke signatures. The various advantages which are related with the AI based stroke detection such as timely and faster diagnosis leading to early treatment and higher accuracy which surpasses the traditional methods. Even the chances for remote patient monitoring have been increased due to AI which also has paved the way for incorporating AI in clinical environments without causing any disruption to current healthcare practices. Further, this chapter discusses the potential of using AI in personalized medicine where the risk assessment and treatment plans for the patient can be based on the medical history of the patient. The chapter further discusses about the long term efficacy of using AI models with the ongoing learning by making use of advances in medical knowledge and access to the data. This chapter ensures to guide the researchers and medical professionals with the deep understanding of using deep learning and AI for stroke diagnosis by exploring the potential benefits, challenges and future outlook for the methodology for early store detection.

Writing technologies shape writing processes and practices. This was true of word processing, speech recognition, and writing with internet-based sources, each of which changed how writers produced and revised text. Generative AI may have an even more fundamental impact because it can participate directly in producing, evaluating, and transforming text. In this study, we examine how generative AI affects the revision processes of professional editors. Six professional editors revised four Dutch business letters with ChatGPT available alongside Word. Using Inputlog process data, ChatGPT interactions, interim texts, and interviews, we reconstructed when and how editors used the model, what revision work they assigned to it, and how generated material entered subsequent editing. Editors used ChatGPT mainly to generate candidate repairs, from complete rewrites to local reformulations, and sometimes to help identify problems in the source text. They differed, however, in when they turned to the model and in how much revision they had already done themselves. Most evaluation, adaptation, and integration still took place in Word. ChatGPT replaced particular revision activities rather than the editing task as a whole. Editors still had to define problems and goals, judge the model’s output, and decide what to retain in the final text. We discuss what these changes mean for how professional revision is organized and for the role of editorial expertise in AI-supported editing.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming healthcare delivery, clinical decision-making and health system governance. However, the safety and effectiveness of AI implementation depend not only on technological infrastructure but also on workforce preparedness and institutional capacity. This conceptual study explores the role of medical universities in Uzbekistan in developing competencies required for responsible AI adoption in clinical practice, healthcare management and public health. Drawing on international literature, policy frameworks and national academic discourse, the paper proposes a conceptual model explaining how educational interventions influence professional readiness for safe AI integration. The analysis highlights persistentcompetency gaps, the mediating role of universities in shaping professional attitudes and broader system-level implications of AI literacy programmes. The study argues that competency-oriented educational strategies aligned with national digital health reforms may support sustainable innovation while preserving professional accountability and patient safety.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education classrooms has reignited the debate over the role of communication between educators and students. This mini-review synthesizes the role of instructional communication constructs (immediacy, rapport, clarity, and credibility) and the relational functions they deliver in AI-mediated classrooms, based on 32 peer-reviewed studies published after 2023, identified through a large-scale literature search (using Scopus and Web of Science-based indexes, OpenAlex, and ERIC). The findings fall into three main categories. First, educator communication behaviors continue to predict student outcomes; a recent meta-analysis reports a moderate-to-large association (r = 0.443), although the evidence base is concentrated in Chinese and EFL samples. Second, students evaluate AI agents using human communication categories, but a systematic gap emerges in the dimension of goodwill, which is partially bridged by cues of immediacy and politeness. Third, when AI replaces human interaction, negative outcomes related to loneliness and a sense of belonging are observed. These three strands are integrated around the complementarity-substitution axis defined at the level of relational functions; tests of measurement invariance, sample diversity, and longitudinal designs are recommended for future research.

This chapter examines the major emerging trends that are shaping the future of nanoparticle science and selection. It explains that the field is moving beyond conventional one-material, one-function approaches towards nanoparticle platforms that are increasingly multifunctional, adaptive, system-aware, and digitally assisted in their design and optimization. The chapter focuses on three major themes. The first is the rise of next-generation nanoparticle systems, including hybrid and heterostructure materials, stimuli-responsive platforms, layered nanomaterials, porous framework-derived systems, bioinspired nanostructures, and safety-aware designs. The second is the growing integration of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-intensive methods into nanoparticle discovery, synthesis optimization, characterization analysis, and predictive selection. The third concerns the unresolved research needs and technological barriers that continue to limit broader translation, including scale-up, standardization, reproducibility, long-term stability, toxicity assessment, and realistic benchmarking. The chapter therefore positions future nanoparticle selection as an increasingly hybrid process in which mechanistic understanding, experimental evidence, and computational guidance will operate together rather than separately.
topics: Chemical and Physical Properties of Materials

documents.abstract: This article examines CP (Couple Pairing) culture – the fan practice of imagining romantic relationships between fictional characters or celebrities – on Chinese digital platforms, combining media sociology, platform studies, and cultural economy. Rather than treating Chinese CP culture as sui generis, the analysis first situates it within a longer transnational genealogy that includes slash fiction, Japanese yaoi, Western real-person shipping, and queerbaiting, before specifying what is distinctively Chinese about its present sociotechnical organization. Drawing on eighteen months of digital ethnography across four platforms (Weibo, Bilibili, LOFTER, and Douban), interviews with forty-five stakeholders, and comparative analysis of five media properties, the study develops the concept of “emotional capitalism infrastructure”: the algorithmic, interface, and narrative mechanisms through which platforms convert affective fan labor into economic value while still affording participants genuine emotional and social benefits. Findings show that platform affordances shape which emotional practices become visible, shareable, and commercially actionable, and that these practices mutate as they migrate across platforms rather than remaining platform-bound. Gender emerges as constitutive, rather than incidental, to CP culture’s affective logic, and China’s regulatory environment is treated as one variable among several – alongside industry structure and platform design – shaping this transnational cultural form. The article closes with governance implications that weigh consumer protection against the cultural and psychological benefits CP participation provides.

This chapter presents four case studies that illustrate how digital transformation is enacted in different institutional contexts under the new academic wave. The cases are analytical examples of diverse strategic and governance approaches rather than evidence of effectiveness or performance. The analysis draws on institutional documents, interviews, and study visits. The University of Helsinki and the University of Turku represent two complementary Finnish approaches. Helsinki combines a mission-driven digital humanities platform with institution-wide coordination of artificial intelligence (AI). Turku implements a university-wide digitalisation programme that integrates learning, research, partnerships, and staff development. Laurea University of Applied Sciences embeds digital transformation within its Learning by Developing model, where technology supports authentic and workplace-related learning. Mondragon University follows a technopedagogical and cooperative approach. Digital tools are adopted when they support pedagogical goals and are governed through distributed support structures and shared institutional values. Tamkang University links digital transformation to a long-standing culture of futures thinking through an all-cloud smart campus and an institutional generative AI service. The cases show that there is no single model of digital transformation in higher education. Instead, digital-era strategies take different forms, shaped by institutional history, mission, governance arrangements, and educational values.

Employee behavior, performance and organizational success are profoundly influenced by motivation, which is a dynamic and ongoing process within human resources. Unlike many other HR systems that rely on fixed tools or formulas specific to an organization, motivation cannot be confined to a one-size-fits-all approach. This is largely because employees have diverse needs, expectations, values and personal circumstances. Consequently, strategies that effectively motivate employees in one organization or even within a single department may not yield the same results elsewhere. HR managers face the challenge of recognizing these differences and developing a variety of motivational techniques that address the diverse demands of their workforce. Over the years, various content theories of motivation such as Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory and McClelland’s Need Theory have provided valuable insights into the internal factors that drive individuals. These theories emphasize essential needs such as achievement, recognition, responsibility, personal growth and job security as crucial elements of motivation. Conversely, process theories – including Vroom’s Expectancy Theory, Adams’ Equity Theory and Locke’s Goal-Setting Theory – focus on how motivation is activated by highlighting perceptions of fairness, the clarity of goals, expectations of rewards and the individual’s assessment of outcomes. These theoretical perspectives have been significantly supported by empirical research conducted in India and beyond, demonstrating that motivation is influenced by contextual and cultural factors. Businesses that effectively understand and apply these concepts can develop a more motivated workforce. Devoted and effective employees are often the result of proper motivation. Both intrinsic and extrinsic reinforcers can inspire individuals to excel. Intrinsic motivation stems from internal elements such as autonomy, meaningful work, personal fulfillment and opportunities for learning. In contrast, extrinsic motivation is driven by external incentives like compensation, bonuses, promotions and recognition. It is essential to strike a balance between both types for sustained employee engagement. Ultimately, motivated employees tend to be happier, which directly enhances productivity, creativity and overall performance. Understanding the nuances of motivation is not merely a theoretical exercise for Human Resource Management; it serves as a strategic tool that influences long-term effectiveness, organizational culture and employee retention. When employees feel valued, empowered and supported, they are more likely to contribute positively to organizational success.

Modern electrical power systems waste between 35 and 55% of primary energy input through thermal generation inefficiencies, transmission and distribution losses, reactive power deficits, and suboptimal demand-side management. This global inefficiency leads to unnecessary carbon dioxide emissions, wasted fuel costs, limited system capacity, and delayed socioeconomic development. As the world moves toward more renewable energy, more distributed generation topologies, and more electrification of transport and thermal loads, it has never been more important to make sure that every joule that enters the electrical network is used as efficiently as possible. This paper provides a thorough academic examination of strategies for enhancing energy efficiency that are relevant to all phases of contemporary electrical power systems, encompassing generation, transmission, distribution, and consumption. The theoretical basis for energy efficiency in power systems has been set, including thermodynamic limits, power factor, conductor losses, and reactive power compensation. The strategies that were looked at include: advanced generation technologies (combined heat and power, ultra-supercritical steam cycles, and integrated gasification combined cycle); high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission and flexible alternating current transmission system (FACTS) devices; smart grid architectures with advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) and volt-VAR optimization; energy storage systems for curtailment reduction and loss minimization; demand-side management (DSM) and demand response (DR) programs; and artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) applications for real-time system optimization. A techno-economic analysis shows that using these strategies consistently can raise the overall system efficiency from a typical developing-country baseline of 38-45% to 60-68%. This means that 15-26 percentage points of primary energy can be recovered, and levelized energy savings can be achieved that make investment in all technology categories worthwhile. A structured implementation roadmap is provided, ranking strategies by cost-effectiveness, maturity, and deployment timeline. This is a useful guide for power system planners and policymakers in both developed and developing countries.

Large language models are increasingly used to simulate human participants in social and behavioral studies, yet static persona prompting typically maps a participant profile and an experimental scenario directly to a response, entangling stable dispositions with situation-specific interpretations. To address this limitation, we introduce \textbf{SPIN}, a cognitive-affective personality system-inspired inference pipeline for simulating human social-psychological behavior. Specifically, SPIN implements this structured inference process through three zero-shot LLM calls that compile a task-blind participant core, elicit condition-specific cognitive-affective states, and read out decisions from those states, thereby reusing stable personality structure while routing each trial-specific response through an explicit state representation. We evaluate SPIN on two reconstructed social-psychological study families spanning uncertainty reasoning and pluralistic ignorance, across four base LLMs. Compared with blank, demographic, narrative, and chain-of-thought prompt variants, SPIN consistently delivers the strongest overall alignment performance across base LLMs and study families. Ablations and state analyses further show that both personality compilation and structured state elicitation contribute to the gains, and that the elicited states shift interpretably across informational and normative conditions. These results suggest that structured personality-state inference can improve benchmark-level behavioral alignment beyond richer persona descriptions or generic multi-step reasoning.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Global aging and the growing digital divide among older adults require more accessible and inclusive digital technologies. This study, developed as part of the national project “Age-It—Ageing Well in an Ageing Society,” aims to define design guidelines based on the scientific and methodological approaches of Ergonomics for Design and Human-Centered Design, with a view to improving the usability and acceptability of gerontechnology. The methodology adopted combines a systematic review of the scientific literature using the PRISMA framework, a focus group with people over 65, and a workshop with designers to gather empirical data and multidisciplinary design perspectives. Analysis of the results led to the development of a set of guidelines organized into four specific categories: cognitive, sensory, functional, and systemic aspects. These categories reflect the main challenges associated with the interaction between older adults and technology, taking into account factors such as memory, attention, linguistic comprehension, motor skills, sensory perception, and sociocultural barriers. The proposed guidelines aim to support designers, researchers, and companies in developing physical-digital interfaces and devices that are accessible, understandable, and engaging for older users, thereby promoting active and healthy aging. The contribution combines ergonomics and participatory design, bridging the gap between technology and the needs of older people, and lays the foundations for future applications in the field of digital health.

Abstract Hydrological drought forecasting remains challenging due to non-linear propagation processes, temporal subsurface lags, and strong spatial heterogeneity across river basins. Conventional deep learning frameworks routinely train monolithic global networks across entire watersheds, which often induces parameter dilution and obscures localized recovery dynamics. To resolve these challenges, this study develops a novel, two-stage artificial intelligence framework that integrates density-based spatial risk regionalization with Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) deep neural networks. Utilizing multi-decadal anomalies of the Standardized Runoff Index (SRI) and Drought Deficit Volume (DDV), sub-basins in the Zengwen River Basin are first quantitatively clustered into distinct drought risk tiers via DBSCAN. Zone-tailored GRU architectures are then trained on a multi-source fusion of hydro-environmental and anthropogenic drivers to forecast monthly SRI and DDV time series in Stage 1, and derive four operational event-level drought metrics—duration, cumulative deficit volume, maximum monthly deficit, and termination rate—in Stage 2. Empirical findings reveal that Stage 1 predictions achieve exceptional accuracy, with coefficient of determination (R 2 ) values exceeding 0.96, Pearson correlation coefficients (PC) above 0.97, and Mean Relative Errors (MRE) reaching as low as 0.039 for deficit volume estimation. Crucially, incorporating prior risk regionalization reduces prediction errors for second-stage event-level metrics by 65% to 82% compared to conventional non-classified GRU models, with R 2 values consistently remaining above 0.97 across all risk categories. Furthermore, the trained deep learning engine achieves a 175 times computational speedup over full SWAT physical simulations, processing 50 years of basin-wide data in just 14.2 s while maintaining high spatial fidelity. By effectively bridging continuous index projections with actionable event-scale recovery metrics, this risk-partitioned framework offers a robust, computationally efficient tool for real-time reservoir dispatch and disaster mitigation.

AI adoption in higher education assessment has accelerated rapidly worldwide. Despite this widespread uptake, ethical dimensions of AI-assisted assessment remain conceptually underdeveloped, particularly within existing technology-acceptance frameworks that conflate ethical and responsible use. This study aims to examine the factors influencing students' intention and actual behaviour in using AI ethically for assessment support, by extending the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) with three ethics-specific constructs: Ethical AI Literacy, Perceived Risk, and Perceived Accountability, alongside the core constructs. The study employed a quantitative cross-sectional design, collecting data from 267 higher education students in London and analysing the data using PLS-SEM with SmartPLS 4.1. The model explained 64.2% of the variance in Behavioural Intention (R²=0.642) and 47.4% of the variance in Actual Ethical AI Use Behaviour (R²=0.474). Results revealed that Ethical AI Literacy was the strongest predictor of actual behaviour (β=0.410, p<0.001), while Performance Expectancy (β=0.279, p<0.001) and Perceived Risk (β=0.249, p<0.001) shaped intention more strongly than conduct, with Perceived Risk exerting a significant negative effect on actual behaviour (β=-0.257, p<0.001). Behavioural Intention significantly predicted actual behaviour (β=0.235, p=0.002) and significantly mediated the effects of Performance Expectancy, Facilitating Conditions, and Perceived Accountability. These findings suggest that institutions should prioritise ethical AI literacy interventions over compliance-based or risk-focused approaches to meaningfully improve students' ethical AI use in assessment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The need for industrial training media in workshop environments requires presentation tools capable of centrally displaying Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) and Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) system simulations, eliminating the reliance on presentation files scattered across multiple instructor devices. This condition underlies the need for an interactive kiosk based on a 65-86 inch Interactive Flat Panel (IFP) as a centralized digital library in the training room. Standard presentation and web interfaces commonly used are designed for small screens, thus lacking consideration for the ergonomics of user reach on giant displays. This study aims to design and evaluate a local-first interactive kiosk interface that considers users' physical reach and multimedia rendering format trade-offs. The method used is Research and Development (R&D) with a prototyping approach, followed by a descriptive qualitative evaluation through heuristic inspection based on touchscreen design standards and touch emulation testing, given the limited availability of the final panel device for direct end-user testing. The test results prove that positioning the navigation menu (Dock Menu) at the bottom of the screen significantly assists users. Combined with a minimum button size of 48x48 pixels and a scalable virtual keyboard (0.7 to 1.15 scale), this design effectively minimizes the risks of fat-finger errors and fatigue caused by excessive arm reach. Additionally, this research identified technical constraints when rendering presentation files (.pptx) on an open-source offline system. There is a trade-off: using a PDF engine maintains clean visual layouts but sacrifices animation effects. Conversely, the OOXML engine runs animations but is prone to layout degradation. The study concludes that the large-screen ergonomic design was successfully implemented; however, its operational success still requires user literacy regarding the chosen presentation format trade-offs. ABSTRAK Kebutuhan media pelatihan industri di lingkungan bengkel kerja menuntut sarana presentasi yang mampu menampilkan simulasi sistem Mekanikal, Elektrikal, dan Plumbing (MEP) serta Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) secara terpusat dan tidak lagi bergantung pada berkas presentasi yang tersebar di berbagai perangkat instruktur. Kondisi tersebut melatarbelakangi kebutuhan kios interaktif (interactive kiosk) berbasis Interactive Flat Panel (IFP) berukuran 65-86 inci sebagai pustaka digital terpusat di ruang pelatihan. Antarmuka presentasi maupun aplikasi web standar yang lazim digunakan selama ini dirancang untuk layar berukuran kecil sehingga kurang mempertimbangkan aspek ergonomi jangkauan tangan pengguna pada layar raksasa. Penelitian ini bertujuan merancang dan mengevaluasi antarmuka kios interaktif berbasis arsitektur local-first yang mempertimbangkan jangkauan fisik pengguna serta kompromi format rendering multimedia. Metode yang digunakan adalah Research and Development (R&D) dengan pendekatan prototyping, dilanjutkan evaluasi kualitatif deskriptif melalui evaluasi heuristik berdasarkan standar desain layar sentuh serta pengujian emulasi sentuh (touch emulation testing), mengingat keterbatasan ketersediaan perangkat panel akhir untuk pengujian langsung kepada pengguna. Dari hasil pengujian, terbukti bahwa memosisikan menu navigasi (Dock Menu) di bagian bawah layar sangat membantu pengguna. Dipadukan dengan ukuran tombol minimal 48x48 piksel dan keyboard virtual yang ukurannya bisa diubah-ubah (skala 0,7 hingga 1,15), desain ini secara signifikan mampu menekan risiko salah pencet maupun kelelahan akibat jangkauan tangan yang terlalu jauh. Selain itu, riset ini juga menemukan adanya kendala teknis saat merender file presentasi (.pptx) pada sistem offline berbasis open-source. Terdapat sebuah trade-off: penggunaan engine PDF memang menjaga tata letak visual tetap rapi, tetapi mengorbankan efek animasi. Sebaliknya, engine OOXML mampu menjalankan animasi, tetapi rawan membuat susunan tata letak menjadi berantakan. Simpulan penelitian menegaskan bahwa desain ergonomi layar besar berhasil diimplementasikan, tetapi keberhasilan operasionalnya tetap membutuhkan literasi pengguna terhadap kompromi format presentasi yang dipilih.

Background Chinese large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for HIV/AIDS health information, yet their multidimensional performance remains unevaluated. This study systematically assessed five mainstream Chinese LLMs across accuracy, caring, completeness, understandability, and actionability. Methods A cross-sectional evaluation was conducted using 50 standardized HIV/AIDS questions. Each model's responses were rated by three independent experts on five dimensions, including adapted PEMAT-based items. Latent profile analysis (LPA) and partial correlation network analysis were employed to identify quality typologies and interdimensional dependencies. Chi-square tests examined associations between profile membership and model identity or question domain. Results The four general-purpose LLMs showed high accuracy (mean > 4.5/5) and completeness (86%−98% full marks), with no significant differences among them (all P-FDR > 0.05). HuatuoGPT-II, the only medical-domain-specific model, scored significantly lower on both dimensions (all P < 0.001). Its responses were less consistent with current guidelines and included one instance of implicit stigmatizing language. All models showed systemic deficits in caring (median = 3.0/5) and actionability (max = 1.70/3). Understandability showed a ceiling effect and no significant profile-level differences, although small model-level differences were observed. LPA identified four profiles: High Accuracy and Completeness (50.0%), Moderate-Balanced (3.6%), Low-Quality (18.8%), and High Completeness and Actionability-Oriented (27.6%). Network analysis identified completeness as the most central node (strength = 0.813) and actionability as a key bridge (betweenness = 0.167). A weak negative partial correlation between accuracy and actionability ( r = −0.083) suggested a potential trade-off between technical precision and practical guidance at the statistical level. Profile distributions differed by model (χ 2 = 124.99, P < 0.001) but not domain ( P = 0.625), indicating heterogeneity stems from model-specific characteristics. Yuanbao-Hy3 showed the most balanced humanistic-technical profile. DeepSeek-V4 excelled technically but lacked caring. Conclusions In this evaluation, the four general-purpose models outperformed the single medical-domain-specific model examined in factual accuracy and completeness. However, systemic deficits in empathetic communication and actionable guidance persist. Model selection should prioritize holistic profile distributions over single-dimension scores. Developers must integrate de-stigmatizing corpora and action-oriented alignment; clinicians should position AI as supplementary to professional care. Future evaluations should adopt person-centred, multi-turn, and real-user validated frameworks.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, including medical education, particularly for research training and academic writing. Research methodology and biostatistics courses are often perceived as challenging, with students reporting difficulty structuring research proposals, interpreting statistical concepts, and applying theoretical knowledge to research practice. This study aimed to assess the perceived benefits, challenges, ethical considerations, and implementation needs associated with a customized AI tool for research proposal writing among fourth-year medical students enrolled in a Research Methodology and Biostatistics course. Methods A convergent mixed-methods design was used. A customized ChatGPT-based Research Proposal Smart Tool (RPST-GPT) was developed and provided to students to support proposal development. Data were collected through a self-administered questionnaire assessing perceived benefits, challenges, and ethical awareness related to AI use in research proposal writing, together with open-ended questions exploring students' recommendations for future AI integration. Results A total of 228 students participated. Students reported high perceived benefits of AI use in research proposal writing (mean 46.48 out of 60) and high ethical awareness regarding appropriate AI use (mean 14.32 out of 20), reflecting recognition of responsible practices and avoidance of overreliance. Qualitative responses indicated that students viewed AI as a supportive learning tool requiring foundational AI literacy and ethical guidance. Conclusions A customized AI tool can enhance undergraduate medical students' research skills when embedded within a structured and governed curriculum. Intentional integration, supported by training, clear policies, and active faculty involvement, is needed to maximize educational benefits and mitigate potential risks.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: We assessed the value of two live human-AI interactions in a precision disease control project in California vineyards. The project tested whether 2021-2024 commercial scouting records and remote-sensing measurements across 140 hectares could support 2025 red-leaf symptom forecasting for prioritized scouting and virus testing. In Workflow 1, Aleks v1, a multi-agent research system, developed forecasting models with iterative human refinement. We applied Aleks's 2024 vine-scale model to updated 2025 predictors and evaluated red-leaf forecasts against independent 2025 scouting. In retrospective simulations surveying 45% of all vine positions, adding model-informed row prioritization to adaptive scouting increased the encountered proportion of newly recorded red-leaf observations from 85.8% to 94.1%. Within-block scouting comparisons suggested the model mainly improved scouting allocation among blocks. Despite unreliable internal 2024 performance estimates from synthetic oversampling before train/test splitting, Aleks developed an informative vine-scale model in 145 minutes, increasing throughput and answering our research questions. In Workflow 2, we assessed whether higher model-score vines had more frequent virus detection, and whether Aleks could infer this sampling goal from a general prompt with data and literature. Aleks's plan prioritized balanced vineyard and model score coverage, while our plan prioritized field efficiency and high-model-score oversampling. Aleks's and our plans yielded 41/50 (82%) and 97/100 (97%) sampled vines. Aleks's plan omitted instructions for replacing missing vines, limiting implementation and operational value. Five of 137 sampled vines tested positive for grapevine red blotch virus (model score ROC AUC 0.735). These findings support assessing AI interactions by how well they advance field research objectives under live, project-specific constraints.

Agentic social networks expose autonomous agents to large volumes of potentially malicious content, including prompt injection, social engineering, and unsafe execution requests. Large Language Model (LLM) judges can detect such content, but applying them at platform scale is expensive. We study the extent to which lightweight embedding-based prefilters can reduce this cost while retaining most of the judge’s unsafe predictions. We annotate 10,000 Moltbook posts and comments with a frontier LLM judge, assigning a binary safety verdict, severity level, malicious intent taxonomy labels, and Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) AI risk codes. Of the LLM-annotated samples, 9.2% were unsafe at severity 3 or above. Two human annotators with high inter-rater agreement (Cohen’s κ=0.823) exhibited moderate agreement between their adjudicated labels and the LLM ratings (κ=0.578). We compare centroid-based cosine prefilters over 3 off-the-shelf encoders against a supervised trained classifier. Reducing the input window size raises average precision by up to 6.3 percentage points. At an operating point calibrated to 0.80 recall, the projected cost of scanning 787,226 messages falls from $7085 by 49.9% (MiniLM-L12-v2), 55.6% (BGE-M3), and 65.6% (trained classifier), while MiniLM runs roughly 32 times faster than the classifier. Prefiltering can therefore make frontier-judge screening affordable at scale, although jailbreak content remains the hardest category to retrieve.

PURPOSE/OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning tool can enhance students' confidence, understanding, and overall experience in removable partial denture (RPD) design. The study also explored student perceptions of AI within dental education. METHODS: A mixed-methods study was conducted involving Undergraduate Dental Technology and Prosthetics students and Undergraduate and Postgraduate Dentistry students with prior training in RPD design. Of the 40 students invited to participate, 35 completed the study. Participants independently completed conventional RPD designs before using an AI-assisted RPD design tool that generated design suggestions based on prosthodontic design principles for comparison and reflection. Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires containing Likert-type items and open-ended questions were administered using Qualtrics. Quantitative data were analyzed using non-parametric tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to assess pre- and post-survey differences within participants, while the Mann-Whitney U test was used to compare post-survey responses between Dentistry and Dental Technology and Prosthetics students and between clinical-based and laboratory-based student groups. Analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS. Qualitative responses from the open-ended questions were reviewed and grouped into four thematic categories to identify recurring perspectives and experiences related to the use of the AI-assisted RPD design tool. RESULTS: Students showed significant improvements in confidence and understanding following use of the AI tool. Items related to the tool's effectiveness, design experience, and visualization received positive ratings, with median scores of 4 (interquartile range [IQR] 3-4), 4 (IQR 4-4), and 4 (IQR 4-5), respectively. Willingness to use AI and perceived helpfulness remained stable, likely due to high baseline attitudes. Qualitative findings supported the quantitative results, with participants highlighting the tool's value for visualizing RPD frameworks and guiding design decisions, while also identifying usability challenges and limitations in design flexibility. CONCLUSION: The findings indicate that the AI-supported tool contributed positively to RPD design learning by enhancing student confidence and conceptual understanding. While it does not replace manual or clinical skill development, the tool shows clear potential as a complementary educational resource that helps bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application. Further research involving larger cohorts is recommended to confirm and expand upon these findings.

documents.abstract: Abstract The increasing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into human resource management has transformed traditional performance appraisal through data-driven evaluation, continuous feedback, predictive analytics, and automated decision-making. This study evaluates the impact of AI-enabled appraisal practices on millennial career advancement, with particular emphasis on gender equality in Mumbai workplaces. It examines AI-supported performance evaluation, feedback, competency assessment, and data-driven appraisal decisions in relation to career growth, promotion opportunities, professional development, and advancement. It also considers whether perceived gender equality and fairness are associated with career advancement and mediate the relationship between AI-enabled appraisal practices and career advancement. The study adopts a quantitative approach using a structured questionnaire among millennial employees in selected Mumbai workplaces. The findings indicate positive relationships among AI-enabled appraisal practices, perceived gender equality/fairness, and career advancement. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI in HRM by connecting technology-enabled appraisal, career development, and gender equality. It also highlights the importance of transparency, consistency, human oversight, and ethical governance when implementing AI-supported appraisal systems.

documents.abstract: EVE-COVARA 2.0 is a proof-bearing and executable research framework for recursive self-improvement (RSI), continual AI adaptation, machine memory, dormant-capacity allocation, and auditable self-modification. Its central objective is to formalize a problem that becomes critical in self-improving AI systems: when may a previously validated adaptation decision be safely reused, when must it be recomputed, and when must the system expand or renew its functional capacity? PureOne/EVE-COVARA-2-Certified-RSI-Research · Datasets at Hugging Face The framework combines protected model editing, recoverability-aware memory, reserve-capacity valuation, covariance-sensitive certificate continuation, nonlinear capability protection, finite-sample acceptance tests, and bounded recursive search. Its strongest mathematical contribution is a noncommutative square-root transport bound for low-rank reserve value under multiplicative geometric drift, together with a quadratic opening result near zero reserve value. This allows cached adaptation and recovery decisions to be transported through controlled model changes with explicit validity intervals rather than being blindly reused or recomputed after every update. EVE–COVARA 2.0 also develops a closed-witness memory architecture in which a compact evidence representation can support an entire declared family of reserve and recovery queries, as well as uncertainty-aware minimax reserve allocation, minimum required reserve rank, information-deletion liability, certificate renewal rules, and second-order nonlinear protection. For nonlinear models, the release includes a correction mechanism that reduces protected-output drift from the usual local \(O(\|\Delta\theta\|^2)\) regime toward \(O(\|\Delta\theta\|^3)\) under explicit compatibility and derivative-bound assumptions. The release is designed specifically for AI researchers, RSI researchers, self-improving-agent developers, continual-learning researchers, and AI systems interested in proof-carrying or auditable adaptation. It includes the full manuscript, reference implementations, locked experiment protocols, raw results, machine-readable claim manifests, negative results, provenance, AI-agent ingestion files, and reproduction tooling. The finalized release records: 138/138 internal numerical and unit tests passed 5 exact final neural certificate witnesses 70/70 fresh counterfactual mechanism-attribution contrasts confirmed 5.30459× median CPU speedup in the declared compiled reserve-query workload 86.65% decision reuse with zero recorded decision mismatches in that workload a 100-step long-horizon recursive-search experiment, in which only two modifications were accepted, explicitly showing that sustained recursive compounding has not yet been demonstrated The framework intentionally preserves unfavorable and null results. It does not claim that general RSI, artificial superintelligence, sustained intelligence explosion, frontier-model superiority, or worldwide priority for the overall architecture has been established. Instead, it provides a mathematically explicit and falsifiable substrate for studying whether recursive AI development can become more efficient, more reliable, and more auditable across successive generations of self-modification. The intended next stage is an equal-compute evaluation on pretrained models or autonomous AI-research agents, where COVARA must demonstrate that certificate reuse saves more computation than certificate maintenance costs, preserves hidden held-out capabilities, and produces descendants that are measurably better at generating further independently validated improvements.
